rolesData.context: Independent consultancy helping retailers and suppliers find margin in assortments, sourcing, inventory, and selling space.
rolesData.about: More Margin Co. works with retailers and suppliers on assortments, sourcing, inventory, and selling space. The work includes product decisions, stores, and reporting.

chapters.text: I work with longstanding contacts on products, assortments, and stores. That can mean helping a supplier reach retailers or working through what a retailer should carry. With DJI, I worked with the home office in China on store standards for its US flagship on Fifth Avenue in New York.
chapters.cap: DJI Fifth Avenue — the US flagship, built to a new store standard.

chapters.text: I enjoy figuring out where a product could go next. With NuvoMed, the work was getting the line into active sports retail: how to position it, where it fit in the assortment, and which conversations to have with buyers.
chapters.cap: NuvoMed — into the active sports retail market.

chapters.text: Retailers also come to me with questions about their shelves: what to carry, how to price it, and what to stop buying. I bring the experience from building private-label ranges to those decisions, working through the products and numbers with the business.
chapters.cap: Assortment planning across a roster of clients.

chapters.text: Some clients need a clearer way to see what is happening in their business. I build dashboards that help them use the information they already have and make decisions before the month closes. It is another way to turn a question into something useful.
chapters.cap: Dashboards built so operators can act on their own numbers.

rolesData.role: Director of Sourcing, Retail, Aftermarket & E-Commerce
rolesData.context: Family-owned Texas RV dealership group, among the largest in the U.S.
rolesData.clientsIntro: I joined to develop private-label products and redesign the stores. Working through that brief also took me into e-commerce, logistics, and the systems behind the retail business.

clients.name: Planning the new stores
clients.did: I drew on longstanding supplier relationships to plan a newly branded Fun Town RV store, with a larger retail offer alongside the RVs on the lot.

clients.name: First newly branded store
clients.did: I developed the merchandising plan, POS, product database, mobile checkout, and website. The 65,000 sq ft store also fulfilled orders for our own site, Amazon, eBay, Walmart, Target, and other marketplaces.

clients.name: Private label products
clients.did: I identified the 60 best-selling items and sourced them directly from factories under two house brands. Margin on those products went from 28% to 79%.

clients.name: Logistics
clients.did: I moved products into third-party logistics and built a portal for stores and head office to place orders, with automatic replenishment in the background. It reduced overhead and errors and made accounting easier.

rolesData.about: One of the largest privately held RV dealership groups in the United States, with a rapidly expanding multi-state network. Sells new and pre-owned RVs alongside parts, accessories, service, financing, and e-commerce — a high-volume retail model that has made it one of the nation's leading towable RV dealers.

chapters.text: I joined to create a 65,000 sq ft prototype store, the largest the company had built. The brief covered branding, layout, merchandising, products, POS, and inventory. There was plenty to connect: each location had its own parts catalog, retail sales ran through an RV financing platform, buying went through distributors, and the products were not visible online. I drew on longstanding vendor relationships to work through the new store concept.
chapters.cap: Planning a 65,000 sq ft store and the systems to support it.

chapters.text: I built a 30,000+ SKU database and worked through the systems around it: POS, mobile checkout, internal ordering, the website, and the first planograms and merchandising standards. The flagship also became a fulfillment center, shipping orders from the sales floor for our own site, Amazon, eBay, Walmart, Target, and other marketplaces.
chapters.cap: The first newly branded store — retail floor and fulfillment center in one.

chapters.text: I looked at the 60 best-selling items and sourced them directly from factories under two house brands. Margin on those products went from 28% to 79%. The sourcing business reached $3M in under a year, and four prototype stores opened using the new layouts and standards.
chapters.cap: Private label: two house brands, 28% to 79% margin.

chapters.text: I moved inventory into third-party logistics and built a portal for stores and head office to place orders, with automatic replenishment in the background. That reduced overhead and errors and simplified accounting. A brief that began with private label and store design had grown into the systems supporting the retail business. It reinforced how much a good team matters when the work crosses that many parts of a company.
chapters.cap: Logistics: 3PL plus an internal ordering and replenishment portal.

rolesData.context: Miami-based retail consultancy reimagining vacant big-box real estate for owners and lease holders.
rolesData.about: Big Box Group worked with retail, e-commerce, and consumer-product businesses on sourcing, product development, sales, logistics, and operations. Its work connected international suppliers with the needs of retailers and their customers.

chapters.text: I was working with past partners to find new sales channels for their products when another opportunity kept catching my attention: empty big-box stores. A 35,000 sq ft space was too large for a boutique needing 2,000 sq ft, while a single large tenant left the owner dependent on one business. I wanted to work out a different use for the space.
chapters.cap: Finding another use for empty big-box space.

chapters.text: That became the FitBox concept: lease the larger space and divide it into smaller shops, with independent businesses sharing facilities such as reception, lockers, and showers. The idea was to lower the cost of opening for each operator and bring businesses with overlapping customers together. Rent, common-area charges, and the fee for managing shared facilities all had to support the larger lease.
chapters.cap: FitBox: smaller businesses sharing a larger space.

chapters.text: The model spread the dependence across different businesses, so one tenant leaving would not empty the entire property. Alongside that work, I restructured a key client’s sales and logistics operations, improving labor efficiency and cash flow by roughly $1M per year.
chapters.cap: Spreading the dependence across several tenants.

chapters.text: What interested me was making an oversized space useful to smaller businesses. A vacancy could become a 2,000 sq ft problem rather than a 35,000 sq ft one. Working through that idea meant paying attention to both the property economics and how the businesses would operate together.
chapters.cap: Making the space work for the businesses inside it.

rolesData.context: NYSE-listed; the nation's largest RV and outdoor retailer.
rolesData.about: One of the largest RV and outdoor-lifestyle companies in the United States, operating a national network of dealerships, service centers, and retail. Its scale, acquisition strategy, and vertically integrated ecosystem have made it one of the most recognizable and influential businesses in the RV industry.

plStory.t: Start with what the customer needs
plStory.d: Every brand began the same way: a category where we were selling somebody else's label at somebody else's margin. Nepallo came out of fishing and sun protection, aimed squarely at Columbia PFG and Huk. Outfitta came out of active apparel. Before a single sample existed there was a customer, a price tier, a competitor, and a reason to exist — then the identity, the color standards, the hangtag, and the fabric story that had to survive being held in a customer's hand.

An owned brand needs to give the customer a reason to choose it, through the product, the price, or both. Temp360 was the clearest case: rechargeable heated base layers, socks, and glove liners, built around a technology story a customer could understand in three seconds on a shelf. That meant specs written on our side, factory samples, testing, and packaging that sold the feature before the price.

plStory.t: Get it from the factory to the store
plStory.d: The work continued well beyond design. Each line was sourced factory-direct through a vendor network built over twenty years, negotiated, imported, cleared, labeled, warehoused, and allocated across a national fleet of stores. Landed cost was modeled before a single unit shipped, because the margin only exists if the freight math works.
plStory.brands: Grill World · Tow Center of America · camping hardlines

plStory.d: The portfolio kept widening. Marine brought Dockmate for docking hardware, lighting and ladders, Covermate for boat and pontoon covers, a pontoon furniture and hardware line, and Gladiator for towables and watersports. Fishing ran from value combos up to an angler tier of rods and reels. Hunting added value and best-tier fieldwear, Trophy Boss for deer gear, waterfowl and archery labels, and two tactical brands for the shooting customer. Flex came in from the other direction — a West Coast watch and watersports lifestyle brand. Each one needed its own identity, tiering, sourcing, and shelf logic.
plStory.brands: Dockmate · Covermate · Gladiator · Trophy Boss · Flex

plStory.t: Make it work in each sales channel
plStory.d: Each brand ran its own site, its own marketplace listings, wholesale accounts, and the retail floor — one assortment with different pricing rules and content needs in each channel. Margin on private label ran far above national brands, and the owned brands gave customers a range they could not buy elsewhere.
plStory.brands: Forge · Simple Nest · Dockmate · 50+ brands in total

plCats.d: Everyday camp and hike wear, performance active apparel, fishing and sun protection, loungewear, heated and cooled technical apparel, and value sun-and-water goods.
plCats.vs: L.L.Bean, Eddie Bauer, Under Armour, Columbia PFG

plCats.d: Tents, sleeping bags, chairs, cots, canopies, and camp accessories across an opening-price tier, a family good/better tier, and a specialty best tier.
Hard and soft-sided coolers, tumblers, and insulated drinkware, plus a full grilling and outdoor cooking line.
RV interior and home accessories for kitchen, living, bedroom and bath, towing and exterior products including hitches, chocks and levelling blocks, and an unbranded utility line.
Rods, reels, combos, bait, tackle and bags across value and angler tiers, plus docking, biminis, boat covers, pontoon, and watersports lines.
Value and best-tier fieldwear, hunting gear, waterfowl and deer-specific brands, archery, and two tactical shooting brands.

chapters.text: I joined to oversee the acquisition of Gander Mountain after bankruptcy and reopen over 80 stores. Four acquired brands were coming together on a tight schedule with a much smaller workforce. The work included keeping useful knowledge inside the business, settling the merchandising direction, and developing house brands to improve margin.
chapters.cap: Reopening 80+ stores after bankruptcy.

chapters.text: I worked directly with the CEO on strategy, integration, rebranding, products, and merchandising. I created over 50 private-label brands with their own identities and sales channels, and more than 20 category shops-in-shop. Over 80 stores were rebuilt and merchandised, with staff trained, in under 18 months.
chapters.cap: 50+ house brands and 20+ shop-in-shops across 80 stores.

chapters.text: The Gander Outdoors grand opening brought 7.5M+ sq ft of retail space into use. By the 50th store, the company adopted the idea of putting RVs inside the retail buildings, reducing merchandise exposure and bringing the focus back to the core business. Those stores became a model for the format that followed.
chapters.cap: RVs in the box — the format that became the blueprint.

chapters.text: With RV sales moving inside, the Gander Outdoors locations were rebranded to Camping World. The change connected the name on the building with what customers found inside. It was a reminder that bringing businesses together involves the products, the store format, and the people doing the work.
chapters.cap: One brand: Gander Outdoors rebranded to Camping World.

rolesData.clientsIntro: I worked with over 80 operators and companies, joining some inside the business and supporting others with specific projects. Here are a few examples:

clients.name: Red Beard Coffee Traders
clients.did: I worked through the retail program: fixtures, floorplans, branding, logistics, assortment, pricing, and technology. My work also included construction management and lease negotiations.

clients.name: Sweet Pete's Candy
clients.did: I redesigned the store experience, including fixtures, floorplans, and branding, and worked on the logistics, assortment, pricing, and technology behind the candy shop.

clients.name: Bentley's Pet Stuff
clients.did: I worked on fixtures, floorplans, branding, logistics, assortment, pricing, and technology. Reworking the fixture package from over $100K to under $25K per store helped the chain expand from under 20 to over 100 locations.

clients.name: Bowery Kitchen Supply
clients.did: I redesigned the store and worked on product records and reporting. The layout and fixtures needed to make a large, varied kitchen assortment easier to shop.

clients.name: W82
clients.did: I redesigned, remerchandised, and rebranded an 8,000 sq ft Chicago space as seven distinct shops-in-shop, each with its own product arrangement.

clients.name: Denim & Soul
clients.did: I created the concept and rebrand for the acquired denim and apparel chain, covering technology, store builds, and merchandising. I then handed the operation over to ML Fashion.

clients.name: American Tea & Coffee
clients.did: I created the concept and opened the first store in Texas, working through the assortment, store design, and build.

clients.name: The Simple Greek
clients.did: I improved operating routines and developed the retail assortment program across the fast-casual franchise.

rolesData.context: Family office of the Camping World CEO and host of CNBC's The Profit.
rolesData.about: A business development, investment, and operating platform focused on creating, acquiring, and improving businesses across retail, food, manufacturing, and consumer products. Developed new concepts from the first idea through branding, products, packaging, sourcing, and preparation for sale.

chapters.text: I worked across more than 80 operators and companies, from coffee shops and candy stores to pet chains, clothing, restaurants, active sports, and kitchen supply. Each had its own questions to work through. Some were portfolio businesses, others prospective acquisitions, and projects for The Profit also had production deadlines to meet.
chapters.cap: Red Beard Coffee Traders — one of 80+ operators.

chapters.text: I worked inside some businesses and supported others with resources, knowledge, and connections between their operations. I developed more than 15 concepts, covering the business idea, brand, packaging, fixtures, floorplans, sourcing, and products. That included creating American Tea & Coffee and opening its first Texas store. I also worked with The Profit’s production team on builds for upcoming episodes.
chapters.cap: American Tea & Coffee: concept to first store.

chapters.text: Several concepts became physical stores for the show and portfolio companies. At Bentley’s Pet Stuff, I reworked the fixture package from over $100K to under $25K per location, helping make expansion from under 20 to over 100 stores possible. Those practical decisions mattered as much as the look of the stores.
chapters.cap: W82: seven shops-in-shop, one Chicago build.

chapters.text: Working to television deadlines taught me to make an idea clear quickly and then work through what it would take to build it. A storefront drawing was a useful starting point for that conversation. The experience carried into how I approached later projects.
chapters.cap: Making the idea clear enough to move into the build.

rolesData.context: Founder-owned women's fashion boutique chain in high-net-worth Northeast markets.
rolesData.about: A vertically integrated fashion retail and apparel business combining product design, private-label development, international sourcing, merchandising, and multi-unit retail operations. Grew to nine stores in under six months on a high-margin, predominantly private-label assortment, then sold to private equity and continued under ML Fashion Group, which added another eleven locations before the business was folded into a larger group.

chapters.text: My sister and I started COURAGE. b in 2008. We had grown up with our mother in the business, and she had taught us a great deal. We wanted to use that experience to create our own products and keep the margin that came with sourcing them directly. It was a difficult year to start, but we could see an opportunity.
chapters.cap: COURAGE. b — the business my sister and I started in 2008.

chapters.text: The financial crisis made landlords in strong markets more willing to negotiate. We secured discounted leases and opened nine stores in under six months. I ran the business alongside full-time executive roles, working through finance, staffing, merchandising, marketing, production, suppliers, leases, and store development.
chapters.cap: Nine stores in under six months, on crisis-era leases.

chapters.text: We built a production network across France, Italy, China, India, Vietnam, New York, and Los Angeles, matching products to the places best suited to make them. Roughly 90% of the assortment became private label. Developing and sourcing the products gave us much more control over the range and its margin.
chapters.cap: Production across seven locations, sold under one label.

chapters.text: Producing our own range also meant dealing with stock that needed to sell at a discount. We created a separate outlet channel, keeping markdowns out of the core stores. It became the strongest channel by revenue, with net margin close to the full-price stores. The business sold to private equity and continued under ML Fashion Group, which added another eleven locations before it became part of a larger group.
chapters.cap: The outlet channel — markdown revenue that protected core margin.

rolesData.context: Iconic multi-channel specialty retailer — roughly 150 stores plus catalog and web.
rolesData.about: An iconic American consumer-products brand known for bringing innovative electronics, gadgets, and lifestyle merchandise to the mass market through specialty stores, catalogs, and direct marketing. At its peak it operated nearly 200 stores at the intersection of technology, product innovation, gifting, and lifestyle retail.

chapters.text: I joined as Manager for Trend Analysis, a role I thought of as Director of Cool. The board wanted to bring fresh products and a sense of discovery back to a 150-store chain. Finding things customers had not seen before was a brief I could get excited about.
chapters.cap: The Sharper Image floor — a brand built on surprise.

chapters.text: I looked through supplier contacts and blogs for new products, then moved into the Director of Product Development role. The work expanded into product development, store displays, and how products appeared across stores, the catalog, and the website. I worked directly with the CEO on the direction of the business and merchandising priorities.
chapters.cap: New products, built from trend signal to shelf.

chapters.text: I negotiated co-op funding and developed plans across the website, catalog, and stores that generated approximately $1M annually. I also helped develop the licensing business, which continued beyond the stores.
chapters.cap: Connecting the catalog with stores and the website.

chapters.text: That experience connected product discovery with how a customer encounters a brand. A product had to make sense on a shelf, on a catalog page, and online. The licensing work added another way for the brand and its products to reach people.
chapters.cap: Licensing gave the brand another route to customers.

rolesData.context: New York advertising agency; new-business development group.
rolesData.about: Kirshenbaum Bond + Partners — a New York agency founded in 1987 that grew into one of the largest independent advertising firms in the U.S., known for disruptive creative, guerrilla marketing, and media innovation for brands including BMW, Target, Citi, Tommy Hilfiger, and Delta Air Lines.

chapters.text: I joined the new-business development group, working with senior executives to win clients and develop work for existing accounts. I was the point person on a group of accounts we won, starting with Priceline.com. I helped build the pitch by working through the positioning, the competition, and how to explain the opportunity.
chapters.cap: Priceline.com — the pitch that opened the run.

chapters.text: Mrs. Butterworth’s brought a different kind of question. It was already a recognizable brand, so the pitch had to show how it could stay relevant alongside private label and lower-priced alternatives. I worked on connecting the creative thinking with the retail questions: what sells, what earns margin, and what deserves shelf space.
chapters.cap: Mrs. Butterworth's — the first major consumer products win.

chapters.text: The wins also included Diageo, Edward Jones, and Snapple. Moving between travel, consumer products, financial services, and spirits meant getting to understand a different business each time. That variety was a big part of what I enjoyed about the work.
chapters.cap: Diageo — one of the new-business accounts we won.

chapters.text: The Sharper Image became both a client and my next employer. Working on the account took me into the products, stores, catalog, and website, and the business later hired me directly. It was the move from helping explain what a retailer could do to taking responsibility for putting it into practice.
chapters.cap: The Sharper Image — the client that became the next job.

items.name: Retail Operations
items.story: I look at what happens in the store each day, listen to the people doing the work, and check the numbers. Then I work with the team on changes they can understand and use.

items.name: Multi-Unit Strategy
items.story: Across several locations, I look for what should be consistent and what needs to stay local. Training, clear communication, and shared reporting help store teams put those decisions into practice.

items.name: Operational Turnaround
items.story: I start with where the business is losing margin and where work gets stuck. I work with the team on a few clear priorities, simpler routines, and tighter financial control.

items.name: Space Management
items.story: I use product performance to plan floor space, fixtures, and product placement. The aim is to make the store easier to shop and make better use of the space.

items.name: Inventory Control
items.story: I look at what sells, what sits, and where stock is running short. I work on purchasing, replenishment, and stock routines so teams can serve demand without tying up more cash than needed.

items.name: Sourcing
items.story: I work with domestic and international suppliers on product, cost, quality, and delivery. Clear requirements and lasting relationships matter when the product has to arrive as agreed.

items.name: Private Label
items.story: I look for gaps in the assortment where an owned brand can offer the customer a useful choice and improve margin. The work runs from product and sourcing through packaging and placement in the store.

items.name: Product Development
items.story: I work through what the customer needs, how the product fits the brand, and what it must cost. That includes testing, design changes, and working with manufacturers on production and timing.

items.name: Brand Development
items.story: I connect the product, packaging, and marketing around a clear reason for the customer to choose the brand. My work includes new concepts and updates to existing brands.

items.name: Assortment Strategy
items.story: I look at what customers buy, what earns margin, and what no longer belongs in the range. Then I work through what to keep, add, or remove.

items.name: Margin Improvement
items.story: I look across product costs, pricing, supplier terms, sales mix, and stock turnover. The work is to find where margin is being lost and make practical changes without compromising quality.

items.name: Pricing Strategy
items.story: I compare costs, competitor prices, customer demand, and stock levels. Then I work through price tiers and promotions, with regular reviews as those conditions change.

items.name: Vendor Negotiation
items.story: I prepare around what the business needs and what the supplier can deliver. The conversation includes price, shipping, returns, and marketing support, with the longer relationship in mind.

items.name: E-Commerce
items.story: I connect the online store with inventory, orders, and fulfillment. I use sales and customer data to work through how the site and its marketing can improve.

items.name: Acquisition Integration
items.story: I look at how both businesses work and what each does well. I work with the teams to keep useful knowledge, agree on shared routines, and continue serving customers through the change.

items.name: Portfolio Optimization
items.story: I assess the performance and potential of each business or location. That helps frame decisions about where to invest, where a turnaround is needed, and where to consider an exit.

items.name: AI Research & Analysis
items.story: I use different AI systems to research markets, compare evidence, and challenge findings. I check the results against business information before using them to make decisions.

items.name: AI Integrated Tools
items.story: I build software around retail and business problems, including margin and daily work. I define the business rules and system design, then use AI to help build and review the software.

items.name: Workflow Automation
items.story: I map the work first: what repeats, where it slows down, and which tools are involved. Then I work on automating routine communication, reporting, and task management.

items.name: Content Development
items.story: I start with who needs the information and what they need to understand. I develop content for digital channels and stores, keeping the product and brand message consistent.

items.name: Shopify & POS Development
items.story: I work on connecting sales, inventory, and customer information across the online store and the shop floor. Staff need systems they can use, and management needs reporting it can trust.

items.name: Databases & Reporting
items.story: I organize product and operating data into reports and dashboards people can use. The purpose is to make the numbers clear enough to support a decision.

items.name: Adobe, Canva & Office
items.story: I use Adobe, Canva, and Microsoft Office for presentations, marketing materials, merchandising guides, financial models, and project work. The tool depends on what needs to be explained or managed.

aiProjectsData.label: Real-Time Audio · Adaptive Audio Engine · Hardware Link · AI-Assisted Build
bullets: Started as a real DJ app running in the browser — four decks, real audio, MIDI hardware support, track analysis, and saved libraries — and grew into ATOMIQ LIVE 1.0, a complete performance system.

The Adaptive Audio Engine is the system's shared clock: decks, waveforms, stems, hardware lights, and visuals all stay in time with the music's phrase, key, and energy. The software spots the moment; the DJ makes the call.

Tested like serious software: hardware control passed 400/400 checks three runs in a row, the interface 489/489, and the intelligence layer 433/433 — with mix scoring proven against a 5,000-track library.

The intelligence picks the best next track, explains exactly how to mix into it, and can even mix on its own — but the moment the DJ touches a fader, control snaps back instantly. It helps the performer, never replaces them.

The product site, the live browser booth (desktop and phone), hardware connections, video output for the crowd, and one unified music library were all built with AI as the tools (Grok + Claude) — directed like a product team, not generated as a mockup.

aiFlowData.name: Define the business problem

aiFlowData.output: A reuse, connect, or build decision

aiFlowData.name: Agree what the tool must do
aiFlowData.desc: Write down the users, the steps, the screens, and what a useful result looks like.

aiFlowData.name: Map the system
aiFlowData.desc: Work through how information moves, which tools connect, and where people make decisions.

aiFlowData.output: Work that can move in parallel

aiFlowData.name: Keep the work in one place
aiFlowData.desc: Save the code, decisions, and handoffs in GitHub so the next person can follow what happened.

aiFlowData.name: Build and connect in small pieces
aiFlowData.desc: Put one useful part in place, check it, and connect it to the next.

aiFlowData.name: Test the actual work
aiFlowData.desc: Check the numbers, the steps, and what happens when something goes wrong.

aiFlowData.name: Review before release
aiFlowData.desc: I review the important decisions and the result before it goes into use.

aiFlowData.name: Use it and improve it
aiFlowData.desc: Learn from the people using it, remove friction, and carry that learning into the next version.

aiStoryData.title: It starts with a working session
aiStoryData.lead: Every build opens as a conversation about a real business problem. One AI shapes the architecture and product direction; another pressure-tests the reasoning before anything is committed.

aiStoryData.title: The research goes wide
aiStoryData.lead: Independent agents scan the market, the competition, and the evidence from different angles — so no single model's blind spots decide anything.

aiStoryData.title: Design becomes working prototypes
aiStoryData.lead: Interfaces are designed as real, clickable prototypes — not static mockups — then packaged into clear communication for stakeholders.

aiStoryData.title: Several builders work at once
aiStoryData.lead: Implementation runs in parallel: multiple coding agents build separate parts of the system in their own lanes, under one set of standards.

aiStoryData.title: Everything lands in one place
aiStoryData.lead: GitHub is the durable source of truth. Every branch, decision record, handoff, and automated check lives in the repository — nothing important stays in a chat window.
